column1: “The war and related events are creating additional upward pressure on inflation and are weighing on global economic activity.” In response, the FOMC’s move to a 3.75–4.00 percent target for the federal funds rate and continued balance-sheet reduction is consistent with standard policy prescriptions in the literature: a Taylor-rule style reaction implies raising the nominal policy rate more than one-for-one with inflation to restore a positive real rate and re-anchor expectations, supporting the 2 percent inflation objective and credibility over time (Taylor; Woodford; inflation-targeting frameworks). Choosing the funds rate as the operating instrument rather than monetary aggregates aligns with Poole’s insight under money-demand volatility. The planned runoff of Treasuries and agency MBS tightens via the credit channel (Bernanke/Gertler). While the Committee acknowledges policy lags and cumulative tightening—suggesting some gradualism under uncertainty—the literature also warns that insufficient response to supply (cost-push) shocks risks unanchoring inflation expectations (Clarida–Galí–Gertler; Orphanides on mismeasurement). Net effect: near-term growth headwinds and tighter financial conditions remain, albeit with longer-run benefits to inflation control and credibility. sentiment score = -0.28
